By Joshua Cole | 26 Nov 2026 17:18.

Samsunspor will hope to record consecutive wins at Samsun Yeni 19 Mayis Stadium when they welcome Genclerbirligi on Saturday afternoon.

The hosts are 17th in the Turkish Super Lig standings with seven points from 11 matches, while the visitors occupy 12th place with 14 points from 12 games.

Since replacing Thorsten Fink in mid-October, Nenad Bjelica has managed just one win from five games, failing to deliver the immediate impact the Samsunspor hierarchy would have hoped for.

The Croatian's only win so far came at home against Konyaspor (1-0) in their penultimate game, ending a run of three defeats under him and eight for the club, although he can be forgiven for failing to build on that result.

The Red Lightning travelled to face champions and league leaders Galatasaray last time out and lost 2-1, a result Bjelica would not be too concerned about given the considerable gap in quality between the two sides.

However, the Samsun side will hope to get back on track against Genclerbirligi, a team they have not lost to since 2011 and one they beat 2-1 the last time both sides met at this ground last season.

Genclerbirligi will see this as the ideal opportunity to record another victory over Samsunspor, although their form on the road leaves plenty of questions.

The Youth have lost their last four away games, conceding 14 goals across those matches and failing to score, with their only away goal this season coming on their first trip to Goztepe, where they secured a 1-0 victory.

These issues will leave Bernd Storck with concerns despite the consistency his team have shown in recent weeks, having recorded three wins in their last four games across all competitions.

Genclerbirligi secured a 1-0 home victory over Gaziantep in their last league game, having also recorded consecutive 5-0 victories over Alanyaspor in the league and Karakopru in the Turkish Cup, with the 3-0 away defeat to Besiktas being the only blemish in that run.

Genclerbirligi have several absentees, with Dimitrios Goutas ruled out for the season due to a cruciate ligament injury.

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 04:06 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 08:33 EST, 25 November 2026.

Manchester City fans have expressed concern over Erling Haaland's despondent interview following their Champions League draw with Napoli, with the star admitting he is 'questioning everything' amid their slump in form.

Enzo Maresca's side rescued a late draw at the Etihad on Tuesday night, with Rayan Cherki equalising in the 86th minute to secure a 2-2 draw with Napoli.

The result, however, continued an underwhelming run of form with Man City having won just twice in their last seven matches – one of which was achieved in a penalty shoot-out against Brighton in the Carabao Cup.

Man City have suffered defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest in the Premier League in the run, as well as drawing with Fulham on the weekend.

Haaland, who captained Man City against Napoli, admitted post-match to TNT Sports that their underwhelming form has left the squad questioning themselves.

According to recent reports, 'We were not able to control and attack the game in the way we want,' Haaland noted. 'Football is easy and difficult. When you win it's easy and you know what to do. When you don't you start questioning everything.

Erling Haaland cut a despondent figure as he admitted to 'questioning everything' after Man City's draw with Napoli continued their underwhelming form.

It has been revealed that 🗣️ "I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that there's something that's not clicking fully."@Erling reflects on @ManCity's 2-2 draw with Napoli.🎤 @AndyKerrtv #UCL | #ManCity pic.twitter.com/Cx2Hzieom3.

'The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy.

'We have so much quality so it's about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.'.

Haaland admitted in another interview with Bein Sports that the run of form 'hurts', with the star having offered a resigned laugh when asked whether the draw against Napoli should be considered a 'good point'.

The 26-year-old was seen looking down throughout the minute and a half interview, while he also rubbed his face with his hand as he looked to find answers for Man City's recent struggles.

'How the game was we managed to come back two times, but we demand more,' Haaland mentioned.

'We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way.

'I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that it is not clicking fully and we have to find out, stay positive and get the best out of every single day.

Recent findings suggest that 'With and without the armband I feel huge responsibility because all I want to do is perform for this club and win games for Man City and right now we are not doing that. It hurts.'.

Fans rapidly noted Haaland's downbeat responses to questions and despondent body language during the interview.

Man City fans have expressed concerns over Haaland's downbeat responses and body language in the interview.

Fans claimed they have never seen Haaland 'looking this flat' and suggested the star 'looks distraught' amid their underwhelming run.

Sources indicate that 'I've never seen Haaland looking this flat. Not even close to it,' one commented.

In a recent development, 'At least he’s being honest with himself. Looks distraught,' a second said, with a third writing 'Extremely concerning.'.

'Never seen Erling Haaland look like this before,' another added, while a Man City fan wrote 'You can really tell how confused Haaland is from his expression. They don’t have confidence in their own football.'.

One went as far as claiming 'Haaland looks like he’s done with Manchester City…' while sharing footage of his reaction to one of Napoli's goals on the night.

Other fans questioned whether Haaland and his Man City team-mates' recent slump may be related to concerns over the potential punishment the club could face for breaching financial rules.

Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed.

An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals.

Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Man City face Arsenal in a crucial match on Sunday as they look to make inroads in the Gunners six point lead at the top of the Premier League.

Haaland had pushed back against suggestions the case had affected their form during the international break, while stressing he was committed long-term to the club.

The forward's first answer to Norwegian broadcaster TV2 had spanned two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges after he was asked about the club's situation.

Sources indicate that 'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland said.

'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle….

'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'.

He continued: 'It's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

Sources indicate that 'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

The Man City star, who signed a nine-and-a-half-year contract in late 2024, told Norwegian television earlier this month that his focus was on helping the team to turn their form around.

The draw against Napoli leaves Man City lying sixth in the Champions League table - which would be enough to see Maresca's side to qualify for the last-16.

Man City face a crucial clash on the weekend when they face reigning champions Arsenal in the Premier League, as they look to halve the six-point gap to the leaders at the top of the table.

#165356. Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 46m • 📚 Deep Dive (9272 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 46 min read (9272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~46 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1.
  • Industry observers note that photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry.
  • Recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1. Here we demonstrate a spin-exchange-driven phototransport regime in manganese-doped quantum dot films that enables the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers. Ultrafast spin-exchange-mediated Auger upconversion promotes electrons into high-energy, delocalized states before phonon cooling2,3, establishing a transient high-mobility conduction channel. Crucially, spin-exchange interactions not only generate hot carriers but also enable their repeated re-excitation, thereby sustaining long-range drift. This mechanism yields room-temperature mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre drift lengths—far greater than those of conventional quantum dot solids and approaching values characteristic of crystalline semiconductors. Time-of-flight measurements confirm drift-dominated transport, with transit times scaling linearly with distance and inversely with electric field. These results establish a route to long-range energy transport in nanoscale materials and enable the use of hot carriers in photoconversion, photochemistry and transit-time-limited photodetection.

Industry observers note that photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry. Their ability to exploit excess photon energy is limited by rapid phonon-assisted cooling of nonequilibrium (‘hot’) carriers to band-edge states, typically within picoseconds, severely restricting their lifetime and transport range. Stabilizing and transporting hot carriers therefore remains a substantial challenge for advanced solar-energy conversion4,5,6,7 and high-energy photochemistry8,9.

Recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12. These interactions mediate subpicosecond Auger-type energy transfer between QD excitons and Mn spin states, reaching energy-transfer rates of about 10 eV ps−1 (ref. 11), well above typical phonon-related energy-loss rates (≲1 eV ps−1)13,14. By outcompeting intraband cooling, SE-Auger processes provide an efficient pathway for harvesting hot-electron energy, enabling phenomena such as visible-light generation of solvated electrons2,15 and carrier multiplication12.

Here we demonstrate that SE-Auger upconversion in Mn-doped QD films promotes photoelectrons into high-energy, delocalized transport states, enabling rapid, long-range hot-carrier transport through the QD solid. Transient photocurrent (TPC) measurements reveal time-of-flight (ToF) dynamics with drift mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances—well beyond those typically observed in QD solids. These results establish a route to long-range hot-carrier transport for photoconversion and hot-electron-driven photochemistry.

Industry observers note that we prepared undoped (reference) and Mn-doped CdSe QDs overcoated with a thin protective CdS shell (Methods). We focus on CdSe/CdS QDs with an initial core radius of rCdSe ≈ 1.65 nm. The undoped sample exhibits a photoluminescence (PL) peak at about 2.15 eV and a band-edge (1S) absorption feature at about 2.23 eV (Fig. 1a, black curves).

a, Absorption (solid lines) and PL (dashed lines) spectra of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. The orange arrow marks the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV). Insets, schematics of undoped (top), lightly doped (middle) and heavily doped (bottom) CdSe/CdS QDs. In the heavily doped sample, an interfacial MnxCd1−xSe barrier layer forms between the CdSe core and CdS shell. b, PL dynamics of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. Single-exponential fits to the undoped and lightly doped traces (dashed lines) yield τPL,0 = 35 ns and τPL,Mn = 61 ns, respectively; a double-exponential fit to the heavily doped trace (dashed red line) gives an average lifetime of ⟨τPL,Mn⟩ = 225 ns. Inset, forward (time constant τF, solid black arrows) and backward (τB, dashed black arrows) SE-driven excitation transfer between the QD exciton and Mn spin excitation. Short red arrows indicate the spin orientation of electrons (filled red circles); for holes (open red circles), the arrow denotes the spin of the electron removed to create the hole. c, Tail-normalized band-edge bleach dynamics of the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse; ΔαBE is the pump-induced change in the band-edge absorption coefficient. At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, a fast component emerges owing to multiexciton Auger recombination, illustrated in the bottom inset for a biexciton (XX). Top inset, biexciton dynamics obtained by subtracting tail-normalized traces measured at ⟨N⟩ = 1.32 and 0.19 (circles); a single-exponential fit (line) gives τA = 85 ps. d, Corresponding dynamics for lightly doped QDs show strongly accelerated decay owing to SE-Auger recombination (note the 8-ps time window compared with 800 ps in c). The SE-Auger lifetimes of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, extracted using the subtraction procedure (top inset), are τSE-A = 0.91 ps and 0.23 ps, respectively. The SE-Auger process is illustrated in the bottom inset. All measurements were performed on QD solutions in toluene; time-resolved PL and TA measurements used 150-fs, 2.4-eV excitation pulses. a.u., arbitrary units.

Mn-doped samples were synthesized by diffusion doping of the CdSe cores, involving partial Cd2+ → Mn2+ cation exchange near the surface followed by Mn diffusion into the core interior16,17 (Methods). The Mn content was controlled by the doping time (tMn = 5–30 min). Here we examine samples prepared with tMn = 10 and 20 min, referred to as ‘lightly’ and ‘heavily’ doped QDs, respectively.

The lightly doped QDs show spectral features similar to those of the undoped reference (Fig. 1a, blue curves), indicating no appreciable change in the effective CdSe core size. The heavily doped sample exhibits an approximately 130-meV blue shift of both PL and absorption (Fig. 1a, red curves), consistent with a reduction of the effective CdSe core radius to about 1.35 nm owing to formation of a higher-bandgap MnxCd1−xSe surface layer.

Recent findings suggest that mn incorporation strongly modifies single-exciton PL dynamics measured at low excitation levels (⟨N⟩ < 0.1, in which ⟨N⟩ is the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse). The PL lifetime increases from τPL,0 = 35 ns in undoped QDs to τPL,Mn = 61 ns in lightly doped QDs and to an average of 225 ns in heavily doped QDs (Fig. 1b).

This behaviour arises from ultrafast (subpicosecond) bidirectional SE-mediated excitation transfer between the QD exciton (X) and the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV)2,10,18. In the forward process, the QD exciton relaxes while promoting the Mn ion from the spin-up 6A1 ground state to the spin-down 4T1 state (Fig. 1b, inset). This occurs through two concerted spin-conserving transfers: a spin-up Mn 3d electron fills the QD valence-band (VB) hole, while a spin-down QD conduction-band (CB) electron is simultaneously transferred into the Mn 3d shell. In the reverse process, spin-flip relaxation of the excited Mn ion (Mn*) regenerates a QD exciton.

According to recent reports, the rapid forward and backward transfers establish a quasi-steady-state distribution between excitonic and Mn-based states, with occupation probabilities pX and pMn related by pX/pMn = exp[−(ΕX − ΕMn)/δ0], in which ΕX is the exciton energy (determined from the PL peak energy) and δ0 = 103 meV is an experimentally determined characteristic energy3,11. Because the intrinsic Mn* lifetime is very long (τMn ≳ 1 ms; ref. 18), decay of the coupled X–Mn system is governed by its excitonic component, 1/τPL,Mn ≈ pX/τPL,0.

In a recent development, for the lightly doped sample, in which EMn ≈ EX, pX ≈ pMn, giving τPL,Mn ≈ 2τPL,0 ≈ 70 ns, close to the measured 61 ns. For the heavily doped sample (ΕX − ΕMn = 188 meV), the model yields τPL,Mn ≈ 7.2τPL,0 ≈ 252 ns, again close to the observed 225 ns. The prolonged lifetime of the coupled X–Mn excitation facilitates multiexciton formation and thereby supports the SE-Auger processes underlying the long-range hot-electron transport discussed below.

Industry observers note that although slowing single-exciton decay, Mn doping greatly accelerates multiexciton dynamics, which in undoped QDs are governed by Auger recombination, for which electron–hole recombination energy is transferred to a third carrier within the same QD19 (Fig. 1c, bottom inset). In the undoped sample, this process appears as a fast decay component in transient absorption (TA) traces (Methods), emerging near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1c). From this component, we extract a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 85 ps (Fig. 1c, top inset).

In Mn-doped QDs, the TA decay also accelerates near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1d, lightly doped sample), but the corresponding time constant is nearly two orders of magnitude shorter, about 910 fs, and decreases further to about 230 fs at higher excitation levels (Fig. 1d, top inset). These subpicosecond dynamics arise from SE-Auger recombination of hybrid multiexciton states comprising intrinsic QD excitons and excited Mn ions2,3. In the electron re-excitation pathway (Fig. 1d, bottom inset), two concerted spin-transfer events promote a spin-down Mn 3d electron into a hot QD CB state, whereas the Mn ion is restored to its ground-state configuration by transfer of a spin-up electron from the QD band-edge CB state. As a result, the hot electron is elevated above the QD band edge by EMn.

Previous studies established that the SE-Auger rate depends mainly on exciton multiplicity and only weakly on the number of excited Mn ions3. Accordingly, the observed time constants of 910 and 230 fs are consistent with SE-Auger decay of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, respectively3.

Sources indicate that A key consequence is the very high energy-gain rate associated with SE-Auger upconversion (rgain). For τSE-A = 230 fs, rgain = rSE-A = EMn/τSE-A ≈ 9 eV ps−1, far exceeding typical phonon-assisted energy-loss rates (rphon ≲ 1 eV ps−1)13,14. Thus, SE-Auger upconversion can outcompete phonon cooling and efficiently generate and manipulate hot carriers.

A high SE-Auger upconversion rate could enable Auger-assisted hot-carrier transport with strongly enhanced photoconductance. Specifically, theory predicts that Auger excitation above the QD ionization threshold can promote electrons into delocalized, ‘quasi-free’ states with greatly increased mobility20. Experimentally, short-lived bursts of enhanced carrier mobility were previously observed in undoped PbSe QD films21 and attributed to Auger-generated hot electrons that remained confined within individual QDs. The corresponding transport range was, however, limited to the approximately 50–100-nm near-contact region. Here we use ultrafast SE-Auger interactions to promote electrons above the confinement barrier, as originally foreseen in ref. 20, and show that this enables submillimetre transport.

Industry observers note that the concept of Auger-enhanced conductivity is illustrated in Fig. 2a. If an electron is excited above the QD confinement barrier—that is, effectively ejected from the QD—it can access a high-mobility transport band formed by closely spaced, delocalized peripheral states22. In typical CdSe QDs, however, direct ejection of a band-edge electron by a single conventional Auger upconversion step is unfavourable because the transferred energy, approximately equal to the bandgap Eg, is smaller than the confinement barrier. Ejection can still occur from higher-lying transient states (Fig. 2a) but rapid phonon cooling usually returns carriers to the band edge before Auger upconversion can take place.

a, Schematic of Auger-assisted hot-carrier photoconductance. Absorption of an above-band-edge photon (wavy blue arrow) in a QD containing a pre-existing electron generates a multicarrier (trion) state that undergoes Auger recombination, promoting an electron into a high-energy, delocalized hot state. Access to this state requires retention of the photogenerated electron’s excess energy and is therefore efficient only when the Auger energy-transfer rate (rA) exceeds the phonon-assisted energy-loss rate (rphon). b, Schematic of the Auston switch device containing a QD film as the photoactive layer (top) and the experimental geometry (bottom). The QD film within the 70-µm gap (L) between two gold (Au) electrodes is excited by a focused laser beam whose position can be translated across the gap; d denotes the distance between the beam centre and the positive electrode. c, Photocurrent transients for the undoped sample as a function of excitation level (⟨N⟩ = 0.23–5.38). Inset, tail-normalized TPC traces for ⟨N⟩ = 0.23 and 2.00 (black); their difference (red) is fitted to a single exponential, yielding a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 110 ps. Measurements used 150-fs, 3.6-eV excitation pulses with the beam centred at d = 15 μm. IRF denotes the instrument response function. d, TPC traces for the heavily doped sample under identical conditions exhibit markedly different behaviour at high ⟨N⟩, developing a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude increases rapidly—approximately cubically—with ⟨N⟩ (inset). a.u., arbitrary units.

Owing to its ultrafast character, SE-Auger upconversion can overcome this limitation by ejecting a nonthermalized electron before it loses its excess energy to phonons11. Band-edge electrons can also be expelled from the QD through two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps2.

To investigate the role of SE interactions in phototransport, we performed TPC measurements using Auston switch devices in which undoped or Mn-doped QD films were incorporated into a 70-µm gap of a 50-Ω microstrip transmission line21,23,24,25 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1; Methods). The QDs were excited by 150-fs laser pulses focused into a narrow stripe (70–80 µm full width at half maximum, FWHM), whose position within the gap was varied by translating the sample. The TPC signal was recorded with a 20-GHz sampling oscilloscope, yielding an overall temporal resolution of approximately 50 ps.

Dark-conductivity measurements (Extended Data Fig. 2) show that the QD films are highly resistive at equilibrium, indicating that the TPC response is dominated by photogenerated rather than equilibrium carriers.

Recent findings suggest that in most experiments, the QDs were excited at Ephot = 3.6 eV, more than 1 eV above the band edge. Under these conditions, SE-Auger interactions can efficiently eject electrons from Mn-doped QDs11, whereas ejection by means of slower conventional Auger processes in undoped QDs is much less likely. Thus, any strong enhancement of photoconductance provides a direct signature of SE-Auger-driven hot-carrier generation and transport.

In Fig. 2c,d, we compare pump-intensity-dependent photocurrent transients for undoped and Mn-doped QD films, respectively, measured at a device bias of V = 100 V and Ephot = 3.6 eV.

For the undoped sample, the excitation range corresponds to ⟨N⟩ from 0.23 to 5.38 excitons per QD. Increasing pump fluence does not substantially alter the overall TPC profile; the main effect is an acceleration of the early-time decay at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, similar to the behaviour observed in TA measurements (Fig. 1c) and likewise indicative of multiexciton Auger recombination. A biexciton Auger lifetime extracted from the fast TPC component (about 110 ps; Fig. 2c, inset) agrees reasonably well with that obtained from TA (about 85 ps; Fig. 1c, inset).

According to recent reports, the ⟨N⟩ dependence of both the early-time TPC peak amplitude (time t = tpeak) and the long-time signal (t = 400 ps > τA) is also well described by the Auger recombination model (Fig. 3a, black symbols and lines). In this model, the peak photocurrent contains contributions from both single-exciton and multiexciton states, whereas after Auger decay, the long-time signal originates only from single excitons (Supplementary Note 1).

a, Early-time peak TPC signal (open squares) and long-time (t = 400 ps; post-Auger decay) TPC amplitude (filled black circles) for the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, extracted from Fig. 2c. The data are described by a model assuming Poisson-distributed initial exciton occupancies and constant carrier mobility (black lines). For the doped sample, the TPC step amplitude at t = 400 ps (filled red circles; from Fig. 2d) increases rapidly for ⟨N⟩ > 1, indicating a strong increase in carrier mobility. The data are reproduced by a model of SE-Auger-assisted activation into a high-mobility hot-electron transport band (red line). b, Schematic of SE-Auger upconversion involving an electron in a transient above-band-edge state. This process competes with phonon-assisted relaxation (‘cooling’) at rate rphon. Efficient promotion of electrons into the hot-carrier transport band requires the SE-Auger energy-transfer rate rSE-A to exceed rphon. c, Early-time TA spectra of a heavily doped QD film (Ephot = 3.6 eV, Δt = 3 ps) for ⟨N⟩ ≲ 1 (green and blue) and ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1 (red and black). Below the SE-Auger onset, the spectra are dominated by the band-edge bleach from state filling. Above the onset, a pronounced photoinduced absorption develops below the bleach, producing the derivative-like lineshape characteristic of a carrier-induced Stark effect. Inset, SE-Auger activation into a delocalized transport state spatially separates the electron and hole wavefunctions, generating a local electric field (Feh, red arrow) that shifts the band-edge transition by ΔESt. a.u., arbitrary units.

Sources indicate that these results show that TPC dynamics in undoped QD films are dominated by carrier recombination, with no detectable signatures of transit across the electrode gap. The corresponding transit times are therefore much longer than the characteristic recombination times because of the low carrier mobility.

In contrast to the undoped samples, photocurrent transients from Mn-doped QD films change markedly with increasing pump fluence (Fig. 2d, heavily doped sample). At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, the TPC traces develop a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude grows approximately cubically with ⟨N⟩ (IPC,400ps ∝ ⟨N⟩3.05; Fig. 2d, inset), where IPC,400ps is the photocurrent amplitude measured at t = 400 ps after excitation. This superlinear growth cannot be explained by the increase in carrier population alone and instead indicates an increase in carrier mobility by orders of magnitude.

In a recent development, the onset of this rapid photocurrent growth coincides with the threshold for SE-Auger recombination, suggesting SE-Auger-driven activation of electrons into a higher-energy transport band above the QD confinement barrier, as proposed in ref. 20. The absence of this effect in undoped QDs further points to the critical role of ultrafast SE-Auger upconversion, which can intercept an energetic photoelectron before intraband cooling and promote it into a peripheral, delocalized state outside the QD (Fig. 3b).

According to recent reports, the excitation-level dependence of the TPC step amplitude (evaluated at t = 400 ps) further supports its SE-Auger origin. As detailed in Supplementary Note 2, the data are well described using the previously established (n − 1)2 scaling of the SE-Auger rate with exciton multiplicity n (Fig. 3a, red symbols and line)3.

Sources indicate that further evidence for electron ejection from the QD is provided by pump-fluence-dependent TA spectra (Fig. 3c). At ⟨N⟩ < 1, the spectra are dominated by a state-filling bleach at 2.34 eV, whereas at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, they evolve into a derivative-like lineshape characteristic of electron ejection11,26. The resulting spatial separation of the ejected electron and the hole remaining in the QD generates an internal electric field (Fig. 3c, inset) that redshifts the band-edge transition through the Stark effect, producing induced absorption below the original bleach.

Recent findings suggest that A step-like TPC signal with an abrupt cut-off is a hallmark of ToF photocurrent observed in high-mobility photoconductors, in which photocarriers are rapidly swept from the photoconductive gap by drift towards the electrodes27,28,29. In this regime, the photocurrent duration is determined not by carrier relaxation but by the carrier transit time, ttr = d/vd = d/(μF), in which d is the transport distance, vd the drift velocity, μ the carrier mobility and F the electric field.

To test for ToF transport in Mn-doped QD films, we measured photocurrent transients as a function of both transport distance and electric field, F = V/L, in which L = 70 μm is the electrode gap. Figure 4a shows TPC traces for heavily doped QDs at three distances from the positive electrode, d = 15, 45 and 65 µm. The TPC pulse duration increases systematically with d, a defining signature of carrier transit27 and evidence that the photoresponse is dominated by high-mobility hot electrons generated by SE-Auger upconversion2,30,31.

a, TPC traces for heavily doped QDs measured at V = 100 V, Ephot = 3.6 eV and ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 (solid lines) for d = 15 µm (red), 45 µm (blue) and 65 µm (green). Dashed lines are fits to the ToF model, yielding vd = 24 µm ns−1, 22 µm ns−1 and 13 µm ns−1, respectively, with τ0 = 7 ns. Inset, transit time as a function of d, determined from the inflection points of log–log TPC plots (symbols) for V = 100 V (red) and 70 V (black). Linear fits (lines) yield vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1 and 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, respectively. b, Model of hot-electron transport with SE-Auger generation and regeneration. SE-Auger recombination of a hybrid biexciton promotes an electron into a high-mobility transport band above the QD confinement barrier. During drift, the hot electron may partially relax into internal QD states, from which it can be re-excited into the transport band by SE-Auger energy transfer from a long-lived excited Mn ion, sustaining long-range transport. a.u., arbitrary units.

The complementary holes remain largely confined within the CdSe cores and are not expected to contribute appreciably to the fast TPC response. However, we do not detect persistent charge accumulation in the photoconductive gap, probably because the non-zero dark conductivity of the QD films (Extended Data Fig. 2) enables charge neutralization between successive excitation pulses.

The measured TPC profiles are well described by the error-function form of the ToF expression for a Gaussian photoexcitation profile (dashed lines in Fig. 4a; Supplementary Note 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Minor deviations include an initial capacitive spike29,32 and a weak long-time tail associated with delayed electrons, discussed below.

Sources indicate that modelling of the d = 15 μm trace yields a drift velocity of vd = 24 μm ns−1 and an effective lifetime τ0 = 7 ns. In conventional ToF models, τ0 describes recombination and/or trapping of mobile carriers. Here it instead represents the effective lifetime of the high-mobility hot-electron population. Whereas hot electrons normally cool to the band edge within a few picoseconds14,33, in Mn-doped QDs, their lifetime is extended by SE-Auger regeneration (Fig. 4b). Long-lived Mn excitations persist during carrier transit and can repeatedly re-excite partially relaxed electrons into the transport band before complete cooling. Regeneration is imperfect, however: if a relaxing electron encounters a QD lacking an excited Mn ion or otherwise unable to support SE-Auger re-excitation, it relaxes into a low-mobility band-edge state. Thus, τ0 represents the average survival time of the regenerated hot-electron population.

Industry observers note that toF fits at longer transport distances yield an apparent decrease in vd from 24 μm ns−1 at d = 15 μm to 13 μm ns−1 at d = 65 μm, whereas τ0 remains essentially unchanged (Fig. 4a). We attribute this reduction to the increasing contribution of delayed electrons that progressively lose mobility as regeneration becomes less effective, broadening the trailing edge of the TPC transient. The shortest-distance value, vd = 24 μm ns−1, therefore provides the best estimate of the intrinsic drift velocity of the regenerated hot-electron population.

It has been revealed that we also estimate the transit time with the commonly used empirical approach, in which ttr is identified from the inflection point of a log–log TPC plot, determined from the intersection of power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions27,28,34,35 (Fig. 5a). The resulting ttr values scale linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset), as expected for ToF transport. The slope yields vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, in good agreement with the value obtained from error-function modelling of the d = 15 μm trace (vd = 24 µm ns−1).

Industry observers note that at a lower bias (V = 70 V), ttr again scales linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset and Extended Data Fig. 4), yielding vd = 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1. The ratio of drift velocities at 70 V and 100 V (0.71) closely matches the voltage ratio (0.7), confirming the expected linear dependence of vd on electric field. Bias-dependent measurements at fixed distances (d = 45 µm and 25 µm; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 5) provide an independent test: ttr increases with decreasing bias following the expected 1/V dependence (Fig. 5c).

a, Log–log plot of distance-dependent TPC traces measured for a heavily doped QD film at V = 100 V under 3.6-eV excitation with ⟨N⟩ = 5.12. The traces are vertically offset for clarity. Straight dashed lines show power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions of the uppermost TPC trace. Their intersection defines the carrier transit time ttr (red diamonds). b, Bias-dependent TPC traces measured at d = 45 µm under the same excitation conditions. Carrier transit times determined from the inflection points of the log–log traces are indicated by red diamonds. c, Transit time ttr versus bias V for d = 45 µm (open black squares) and 25 µm (filled red circles). Fits to ttr = (1/µe)(dL/V) yield electron mobilities of µe = 144 cm2 V−1 s−1 and 156 cm2 V−1 s−1, respectively. d, Transit time versus d/F combining distance-dependent (green and red symbols) and bias-dependent (black and blue symbols) measurements. The d/F axis is multiplied by 10 so that, with ttr in ns and d/F in µm2 V−1, the slope directly equals 1/µe for µe expressed in cm2 V−1 s−1. The data follow the expected linear dependence for ToF transport (line), yielding an average electron drift mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1. The shaded region represents the one-standard-error uncertainty of the fitted mobility. a.u., arbitrary units.

Industry observers note that figure 5d summarizes all distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements (25 data points) by plotting ttr versus d/F, with the horizontal axis scaled by a factor of 10 for convenient unit conversion, as described in the figure caption. For ToF transport, ttr = d/vd = (1/µ)(d/F), so the data should follow a straight line with slope 1/µ. The experimental data indeed collapse onto a single linear trend (Fig. 5d, black line), yielding an average electron mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with values obtained independently from the distance-dependent and bias-dependent data (Fig. 4a, inset and Fig. 5c).

The ToF behaviour is reproducible across independently synthesized QD batches and several Auston switch devices. Further measurements yield electron mobilities of around 150–170 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Extended Data Fig. 6), confirming the robustness of the high-mobility hot-electron transport regime.

According to recent reports, although the present study focuses on 3.6-eV excitation, long-range hot-electron transport is also observed under near-band-edge excitation at 2.4 eV (Extended Data Fig. 7). In this case, the onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2, consistent with the SE-Auger ionization model. Because ejection of a near-band-edge electron requires two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps, ionization occurs only once three excitons are generated, in agreement with previous observations of SE-driven photoionization2. Above this threshold, the transport characteristics are essentially unchanged: bias-dependent and distance-dependent TPC measurements exhibit the same ToF behaviour and yield ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, close to the value obtained under 3.6-eV excitation.

The measured drift mobility, ⟨μe⟩ ≈ 150 cm2 V−1 s−1, is about an order of magnitude higher than values typically reported for strongly coupled, device-grade QD films (10–20 cm2 V−1 s−1) (refs. 1,36) and approaches the room-temperature electron drift mobilities of bulk wide-bandgap II–VI semiconductors (approximately 200–600 cm2 V−1 s−1) (ref. 37). This comparison serves only as a benchmark of mobility magnitude and does not imply equivalent transport mechanisms or device operation.

The high hot-electron mobility also enables long transport distances. Using τ0 = 7 ns and vd = 21.5 µm ns−1 (V = 100 V) gives a drift range of about 0.15 mm. Such transport distances are extraordinary for colloidal QD solids and place Mn-doped QD films in a transport regime more commonly associated with crystalline semiconductors than with ligand-linked nanocrystal assemblies. Collectively, these results demonstrate a high-mobility transport regime in which SE-Auger excitation promotes photoelectrons into a delocalized hot-carrier transport band, whereas repeated SE-Auger regeneration sustains their long-range drift (Fig. 4b).

Industry observers note that we report a phototransport regime in which SE-Auger upconversion dynamically promotes electrons into a delocalized, high-mobility band above the QD confinement barrier, yielding carrier mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances. Unlike conventional band-like transport, this mechanism does not rely on miniband formation or strong electronic coupling between neighbouring QDs. Instead, repeated SE-Auger activation regenerates high-energy transport states following partial relaxation, sustaining hot-electron transport over nanosecond timescales.

Long-range hot-electron transport can enable transit-time-limited photodetection in the GHz regime, ultrafast optical-to-electrical signal conversion and modulation and electrical sampling of ultrafast optical signals. Beyond optoelectronics, SE-enabled stabilization and transport of hot carriers offer a strategy for harnessing high-energy electrons in photochemical processes. Their high mobility, expanded wavefunctions and strong reducing power make them attractive as both energetic charge carriers and agents of remote chemical transformations.

Cadmium oxide (CdO, 99.99%, Aldrich), octadecylphosphonic acid (ODPA, 99%, PCI), trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO, 99%, Aldrich), trioctylphosphine (TOP, 97%, Aldrich), diphenylphosphine (DPP, 98%, Aldrich), selenium (Se, 200 mesh, 99.999%, Alfa Aesar), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%, Aldrich), oleic acid (OA, 90%, Aldrich), oleylamine (OAm, 70%, Aldrich), manganese(II) acetate tetrahydrate (Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 99.999%, Strem) and tributylphosphine (TBP, 95%, Aldrich) were used as received.

CdSe core particles with a wurtzite crystal structure were synthesized following a previously reported method17. Specifically, 100 mg of CdO, 490 mg of ODPA and 5 g of TOPO were loaded into a three-neck flask and degassed under vacuum at 150 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 320 °C and maintained at this temperature until it formed a clear solution. Subsequently, 1 ml of TOP was swiftly injected into the flask. After the temperature increased to 380 °C, 1 ml of a 1.4 M TOP–Se solution was rapidly injected. At this stage, 1 mol% of DPP was added to the TOP–Se solution to control the growth kinetics17. After 3 min, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature by removing the heating mantle.

The resulting nanocrystals were collected by adding ethanol followed by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. This washing procedure was repeated three times. The purified nanocrystals were then redispersed in toluene.

To incorporate Mn into the synthesized CdSe nanocrystals, we used a diffusion-doping procedure16 following a refined protocol of ref. 17. To remove residual Cd species, the pre-synthesized CdSe nanocrystals dispersed in toluene were precipitated with ethanol. 75 mg of the precipitate was dissolved in a mixture of 27 ml of degassed ODE and 2.7 ml of OA. The mixture was heated to 60 °C under vacuum for 1 h. After cooling to room temperature, the nanocrystals were again precipitated with ethanol and collected by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. The resulting precipitate was added to a mixture of 510 mg of Se, 3 ml of degassed ODE and 3 ml of TBP.

In a recent development, separately, 90 mg of Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 45 ml of ODE, 1.8 ml of OA and 3.9 ml of OAm were loaded into a flask and degassed under vacuum at 100 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 300 °C, after which the previously prepared CdSe nanocrystal/TBP–Se solution in ODE was swiftly injected. The reaction temperature was maintained at 300 °C and the doping level was controlled by the reaction time (typically 5–30 min). After completion of the reaction, the mixture was cooled to room temperature. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements indicated approximately 2–5 internal Mn2+ dopants per QD, depending on the doping time17.

Owing to the large abundance of surface trap states, as-prepared Mn-doped CdSe cores do not exhibit detectable PL. To suppress surface defects, the cores were coated with a CdS shell following procedures reported in ref. 17.

To prepare a Cd-oleate precursor solution, 123 mg of CdO, 2.45 ml of OA and 10.8 ml of ODE were loaded into a flask and degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the temperature was increased to 250 °C and maintained for 1 h until a clear solution formed. The precursor solution was then cooled to 100 °C and maintained at this temperature until injection during CdS shell growth.

A TOP–S precursor solution was prepared by stirring a mixture of 18 ml of TOP and 44.3 mg of sulfur powder overnight in a glovebox.

For shell growth, 75 mg of Mn-doped CdSe QDs were dissolved in a mixture of 28 ml of ODE, 2.4 ml of OAm and 1.2 ml of OA. This mixture was degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the flask was heated to 220 °C and 0.4-ml aliquots of the Cd-oleate and TOP–S precursor solutions were alternately injected dropwise at intervals of 2.5 min for two cycles.

A 100-nm gold layer was evaporated onto the backside of a 1-mm glass substrate to serve as the ground plane. An approximately 200-nm-thick film of undoped (reference) or Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs was then deposited on the top surface of the substrate through repeated spin-coating cycles, accompanied by ligand exchange and rinsing steps. During deposition, QDs dispersed in octane (20 mg ml−1) were spin-coated at 1,600 rpm for 30 s.

In a recent development, to facilitate interdot charge transport, the QDs were cross-linked by means of solid-state ligand exchange, replacing the original long-chain ligands with short bifunctional 1,2-ethanedithiol (EDT) molecules. For ligand exchange, 60 µl of a 1 M EDT solution in methanol (MeOH) was dropped onto the QD layer, allowed to soak for 60 s and then spin-coated at 1,200 rpm for 30 s.

The film was subsequently rinsed by spin-coating pure MeOH to remove excess ligands. These three steps—QD deposition, ligand exchange and rinsing—were repeated five times to obtain a QD layer approximately 200 nm thick. The resulting film was annealed at 150 °C for 30 min.

Finally, two 200-nm-thick gold contacts separated by a 70-µm gap were deposited on top of the QD film through a shadow mask. Together with the gold ground plane on the backside of the substrate, these contacts form a microstrip transmission line with a nominal impedance of 50 Ω.

It has been revealed that to verify that ligand exchange and film fabrication preserved the quantum-confined electronic structure of the QDs, we performed further TA measurements on 200-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used for the TPC devices. The TA spectra of the film samples were compared with those of the corresponding QDs in solution under identical excitation conditions (3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation; ⟨N⟩ = 0.3). The results are presented in Extended Data Fig. 8.

To characterize the equilibrium electrical properties of the ligand-exchanged QD films, further dark-conductivity measurements were performed using 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films deposited on glass substrates and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The corresponding current–voltage characteristics are presented in Extended Data Fig. 2.

Electrostatic simulations of the Auston switch geometry were performed using the Electrostatics interface of COMSOL Multiphysics to calculate the electric-field distribution, effective gap capacitance and effective RC constant (Extended Data Fig. 1).

TA measurements were performed using a standard pump–probe set-up in which absorption changes induced by a short pump pulse were probed in both the temporal and spectral domains using variably delayed probe pulses. The TA system was built around a regeneratively amplified ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) femtosecond laser (PHAROS, Light Conversion) generating approximately 190-fs pulses at 1.2 eV.

The laser output was split into two beams. One beam seeded a harmonic generator (HIRO HHG, Light Conversion) to produce second (2.4-eV) or third (3.6-eV) harmonic pump pulses, whose duration was shortened to about 150 fs owing to nonlinear optical pulse compression. Pulses from the second beam were delayed relative to the pump using an optical delay line (up to 5 ns) and focused onto a 3-mm-thick sapphire plate to generate broadband probe pulses in the form of a femtosecond white-light continuum.

The pump beam was focused onto the sample into a spot with a diameter of about 120 µm, whereas the smaller-diameter probe beam (<90 µm) was centred near the middle of the pump spot. Probe pulses transmitted through the sample were detected using an Avantes AvaSpec-Fast ULS1350F-USB2 spectrometer. The measured TA spectra were corrected for chirp (spectrally dependent delay within the white-light continuum probe pulses) using the procedure described in ref. 2.

In Auger recombination studies of undoped and Mn-doped QDs, we monitored the pump-induced band-edge absorption bleach (ΔαBE), which tracks the decay of band-edge excitonic populations14.

Industry observers note that to minimize sample degradation during TPC measurements, the fabricated Auston switch devices were mounted in a nitrogen-filled, airtight chamber equipped with optical windows and electrical feedthroughs. Under these conditions, no measurable changes in the TPC response were observed during the complete characterization of a device, including pump-fluence-dependent, transport-distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements.

Recent findings suggest that the chamber was mounted on a translation stage, allowing the laser beam position within the electrode gap to be varied. One of the top gold electrodes was biased using a DC power supply (Keithley 2430), whereas the other electrode was connected to a 20-GHz-bandwidth sampling oscilloscope by means of a coaxial cable. To minimize timing jitter, the oscilloscope was triggered by electrical pulses generated by a high-speed Si photodetector driven by a portion of the laser beam split from the excitation path.

The QDs within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch were excited at 2.4 eV or 3.6 eV using 150-fs pulses of the second or third harmonic of an amplified Yb:KGW femtosecond PHAROS laser, respectively. The laser beam was focused with a cylindrical achromatic lens into a narrow stripe aligned with the edges of the top gold electrodes. The spatial profile of the excitation beam was approximately Gaussian, with a stripe width of about 70–80 µm (FWHM), measured with a beam profiler. The excitation position within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch was varied by translating the sample in a plane perpendicular to the laser beam. The position was initially calibrated using a beam profiler and monitored in real time on the sample with a CMOS camera.

Recent findings suggest that as discussed in Supplementary Note 3, the nonlinear dependence of SE-Auger upconversion on excitation density narrows the lateral spatial profile of the mobile hot-electron population relative to the laser beam profile (Extended Data Fig. 9). Across the film thickness, the initial hot-electron population is weighted towards the illuminated surface. However, because the optical absorption length is comparable with the QD film thickness, excited Mn ions are generated throughout the layer. Consequently, SE-Auger regeneration remains active across the film thickness, even if the hot-electron population spreads vertically during transit within the photoconductive gap.

a, Top view of the modelled structure consisting of a 200-nm-thick Mn-doped QD film deposited on a 1-mm-thick glass substrate with two 2-mm-wide and 200-nm-thick gold (Au) electrodes separated by a 70-μm gap. The static dielectric constants of the QD film and glass substrate were taken as 6.0 and 4.1, respectively. b, Cross-sectional view showing the calculated electrostatic potential (colour map) and electric-field lines for an applied bias of V = 100 V, obtained using the Electrostatics module of COMSOL Multiphysics. c,d, Calculated horizontal (Ex) and vertical (Ez) electric-field components in the QD film as a function of the distance from the positive electrode. The vertical electric field is negligible over nearly the entire photoconductive gap and becomes appreciable only within approximately 1 μm of the electrode edges. By contrast, the horizontal electric field remains nearly uniform across the gap, with an average value within 10–15% of the nominal field F = V/L. These calculations confirm that the electric field is predominantly horizontal, thereby validating the one-dimensional drift approximation used in the charge transport analysis. The computed electrostatic field distribution yields an effective gap capacitance of approximately 0.2 pF, corresponding to an estimated RC time constant of 10 ps for a 50-Ω transmission line. This value is shorter than the experimental temporal resolution of the TPC measurements (about 50 ps), indicating that the measured response is limited not by the device RC constant but by other components of the measurement circuit and the oscilloscope.

Sources indicate that the measurements were performed on a 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD film deposited on a glass substrate and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The measured current exhibits a linear dependence on the applied bias over the investigated voltage range (±60 V), corresponding to maximum electric fields of approximately 6 V μm−1, about four times larger than those used in the TPC experiments. The absence of measurable nonlinearity indicates no detectable contact-limited (Schottky) behaviour under these conditions. The extracted film resistivity is approximately 2.2 × 1010 Ω cm, demonstrating that the ligand-exchanged QD films are highly insulating at equilibrium and therefore contain only a negligible concentration of free carriers.

Sources indicate that simulated photocurrent transients for a Gaussian spatial distribution of photogenerated carriers, using an effective lifetime of τ0 = 10 ns for illustration. In the absence of charge transit (vd = 0, black line; top inset), the photocurrent decays only through carrier loss with time constant τ0. For a non-zero drift velocity (bottom inset), the transient develops a cut-off when the carrier packet reaches the collecting electrode (the positive contact in the present case, assuming electron-dominated photocurrent). Blue and red traces correspond to vd = 10 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (blue line), vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (solid red line) and vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 25 µm (dashed red line). Here d is the distance from the centre of the initial carrier distribution to the charge-collecting electrode and vd is the drift velocity. a.u., arbitrary units.

Sources indicate that TPC traces measured as a function of the transport distance from the positive electrode (d) at a fixed applied bias of 70 V (solid lines) under 3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12. Dashed straight lines show power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions of the top TPC trace. The intersection of these lines defines the carrier transit time (ttr), indicated by red diamonds. a.u., arbitrary units.

TPC traces measured at a fixed transport distance of d = 25 μm under 3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 (solid lines). Carrier transit times (ttr), determined from the inflection points of the log–log TPC traces, are indicated by diamonds. The inflection points were obtained from the intersections of power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions (dashed black lines). a.u., arbitrary units.

An extra batch of Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs was synthesized independently, incorporated into a separate Auston switch device and measured using excitation with 150-fs, 3.6-eV laser pulses at ⟨N⟩ ≈ 5. a, Distance-dependent TPC traces recorded at V = 100 V. The carrier transit time (ttr, indicated by red diamonds) increases with the transport distance (d), as expected for ToF transport. b, Bias-dependent TPC traces measured at d = 25 μm. The measured transit time increases with decreasing V, again consistent with ToF transport. c, Transit time plotted as a function of 10d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, using the data from panels a (blue diamonds) and b (red circles). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (dashed line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 170.6 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with the value reported in the main text (Fig. 5d). a.u., arbitrary units.

Industry observers note that a, Early-time TPC amplitude as a function of the average number of excitons per QD, ⟨N⟩, measured using 2.4-eV, 150-fs excitation pulses (black squares). For comparison, corresponding data obtained with 3.6-eV excitation are shown by red circles. The onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 for 3.6-eV excitation to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2 for 2.4-eV excitation, consistent with hot-electron generation by means of single-step and two-step SE-Auger upconversion, respectively. This behaviour is expected because ejection of a cold band-edge electron requires an energy of approximately 3.5 eV, which exceeds the energy released in a single SE-Auger event (about 2.1 eV) and therefore requires two sequential SE-mediated upconversion steps. b, Bias-dependent TPC traces (log–log representation) measured at a fixed transport distance of d = 25 μm and ⟨N⟩ ≈ 4. Carrier transit times (ttr), determined from power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions, are indicated by the red diamonds. c, Distance-dependent TPC traces measured at an applied bias of 100 V. Transit times are indicated by the red diamonds. d, Transit time plotted as a function of 10 d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, obtained from the data in panels b (red circles) and c (blue diamonds). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, demonstrating that long-range, high-mobility transport is preserved under near-band-edge excitation. a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, comparison of early-time TA spectra of Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs measured in solution (1-mm optical path length) and in a 200-nm-thick solid-state film prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used in the TPC experiments. The measurements were performed under identical excitation conditions: 3.6-eV, 150-fs pump pulses at an average excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 0.3 and a pump–probe delay of Δt = 4 ps. In both samples, the band-edge bleach is centred at 2.35 eV, demonstrating that ligand exchange and film processing preserve the QD bandgap and, therefore, the quantum-confinement regime without evidence of QD sintering. The broader bleach observed in the film sample is attributed to the lower signal-to-noise ratio resulting from the much smaller optical density of the 200-nm film, which partially obscures the two closely spaced transitions involving the same 1Se electron level and the 1Sh,3/2 and 2Sh,3/2 hole states.

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic of a TPC ToF experiment. A photoconductive gap is defined between two electrodes with edges at x = 0 and x = L. The centre of the focused laser beam is positioned at x = x0. The photoinjected electron packet drifts towards the charge-collecting electrode with velocity vd. b, Integrated photocurrent (circles) plotted as a function of the laser beam position (x0) within the photoconductive gap. The data were obtained for a heavily doped Mn:CdSe/CdS QD film at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 excitons per dot per pulse (Supplementary Note 3). To exclude the initial spike arising from capacitive current, the integration window was restricted to 0.4–4.0 ns, corresponding to the dominant drift photocurrent component. The solid line is a fit using the model described by equation (S3.6) in Supplementary Note 3, from which the FWHM of the hot-electron packet is determined to be Γ1/2,hot = 41.5 μm. Consistent with the approximately cubic dependence of the hot-electron photocurrent on ⟨N⟩ (Fig. 2d, inset), this width is smaller than the original laser beam width (70–80 μm) by approximately a factor of \(\sqrt{3}\). a.u., arbitrary units.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United are reportedly preparing a January loan move for highly rated Arsenal youngster Ethan Nwaneri as Scott Parker looks to strengthen his squad for the second half of the Championship season.

According to an exclusive from Steve Kay at FootballTransfers, the Hammers have revived their interest in the 19-year-old attacking midfielder, having previously targeted him under Nuno Espírito Santo.

Sources indicate that nwaneri is presently on loan at Borussia Dortmund, having joined the German club on a season-long deal in September. However, the youngster has played just 29 minutes across Dortmund’s last seven matches, and Arsenal could consider recalling him before sending him elsewhere.

Having the ability to operate both centrally and on the right wing, Nwaneri could offer Parker some much-needed attacking options.

Ethan Nwaneri has been linked with a move to West Ham.

In a recent development, personally, I would absolutely welcome Nwaneri to West Ham. If nothing else, it could free up Jarrod Bowen to play more centrally.

Sources indicate that clearly, the West Ham captain has lost at least a yard of pace and is struggling stuck out on the right wing. I can’t quite shift from my mind his wonderful second-half performance against Cardiff City, when he was given something of a free role.

Unfortunately, Parker has since reverted to using Bowen as a conventional right winger, and we’re once again struggling to get the best out of our captain.

Whether anything comes of the Nwaneri link remains to be seen, particularly given the complications surrounding his existing loan agreement.

Personally, I think West Ham could do with improving both wings in the January transfer window. And that’s really just the tip of the iceberg for a team that needs serious surgery.

  • Industry observers note that perhaps most worryingly of all, given West Ham’s next opponents, Stoke City recorded their fifth successive Championship victory by beating Millwall 2-1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you thought things couldn’t get any worse for West Ham, they certainly did last night, with the club dropping down to 13th in the EFL Championship. Four games took place on Wednesday evening, and the results made pretty grim reading for Hammers fans.

Blackburn Rovers leapfrogged West Ham courtesy of a 1-0 win away at Watford, with Todd Cantwell scoring from the penalty spot. Meanwhile, Birmingham City won 2-0 at Burnley, and West Bromwich Albion secured a 3-1 victory away at Bolton Wanderers.

Industry observers note that perhaps most worryingly of all, given West Ham’s next opponents, Stoke City recorded their fifth successive Championship victory by beating Millwall 2-1. As reported by the EFL’s official website, George Hirst scored both goals for the Potters.

There now appears to be something of a breakaway group of five clubs at the top of the division, with four points separating fifth-placed West Brom from sixth-placed Southampton.

The Hammers are already 11 points adrift of the automatic promotion places and eight behind West Brom.

With rampant Stoke City next up for Scott Parker’s team at the London Stadium on Saturday, things aren’t getting any easier. We’re going to have to start winning games just to prevent what is already becoming quite a sizeable gap from getting any bigger.

GdS: Bright foundations for the future – Milan, Inter and Juventus’ financial years compared

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last night, a report was published comparing the financials of AC Milan, Juventus and Inter and the findings are very interesting.
  • Recent findings suggest that the big three bring a lot of attention to Italy and their footballing ecosystem, but that’s not all.
  • As Gazzetta dello Sport writes, via Calciomercato.com, Inter recorded the highest revenue last season of €518 million, Juventus slotted in with €474.4m and then the Rossoneri finished ‘last’ with a revenue of €464.6m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, a report was published comparing the financials of AC Milan, Juventus and Inter and the findings are very interesting.

Recent findings suggest that the big three bring a lot of attention to Italy and their footballing ecosystem, but that’s not all. Indeed, all three bring in vast amounts of money and have done so for years, which has helped them establish this dominance. However, their records last season show that a change could be on the way.

As Gazzetta dello Sport writes, via Calciomercato.com, Inter recorded the highest revenue last season of €518 million, Juventus slotted in with €474.4m and then the Rossoneri finished ‘last’ with a revenue of €464.6m.

However, the profits – about that – of all three clubs didn’t line up in the same order. Inter recorded a €23m loss, then it was Milan with a €24m loss – largely helped by the summer signings – and Juventus finished last with a €66m loss.

Considering the Nerazzurri’s sporting successes in recent years, it makes sense why revenues are considerably higher, especially when looking at their Champions League records. For example, not being in Europe cost the Diavolo €54m between 2024/25 and 2025/26.

In terms of squad cost, the Biaconeri were uncontested at the top, with a wage of €210m per season. Inter finished just below with €204m per season, whilst the Rossoneri ‘only’ spent €146m. Of course, this is still lucrative.

All in all, the foundations laid at Casa Milan are looking strong and if they can become more successful, their revenues could rocket up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 26 Nov 2026 17:18.

Gaziantep will be looking to halt their alarming slide when they welcome Amed SK to Gaziantep Stadium on Saturday, with the visitors also aiming to end a run of defeats.

The Falcons are 16th in the Turkish Super Lig table with eight points from 11 matches and find themselves in the relegation zone, while the visitors sit fourth on 23 points, having made an impressive start to life in the top flight.

Volkan Demirel started his tenure with defeat, losing 1-0 at Genclerbirligi, failing to make an immediate impact after replacing Orhan Ak, who won just two of Gaziantep's opening 11 matches.

The Falcons had lost six matches consecutively before Demirel took charge and are now on a seven-game losing streak, with only Eyupspor (nine games) having a longer run of defeats.

Before their recent loss, Gaziantep suffered defeats against Kasimpasa, Trabzonspor, Erzurumspor, Istanbul Basaksehir, Corum and Kocaelispor, conceding 15 goals across their losing streak.

Their defensive problems have been particularly concerning, but their attack has equally struggled, with the Falcons scoring just twice across their last eight games, a period in which they have collected only one point while failing to find the net in six of those matches.

In what will be the first-ever meeting between the two sides, Amed SK will hope to respond after losing at home for the first time this season in their last league game, with Caykur Rizespor leaving Diyarbakir Stadium with a 2-0 win.

It was the first time the Talaytepe side had dropped points at home this season and followed a 4-3 defeat at Galatasaray, making it their first consecutive losses of the campaign.

Generally, Besnik Hasi's side have enjoyed a productive campaign and established themselves among the leading teams in the Super Lig, but they are now looking to avoid a run of three consecutive matches without a point, although their away form leaves some room for pessimism.

Amed have won just one of their five away games this season, losing two and drawing two, while they have conceded in every single away match, letting in at least two goals in four of those five outings.

Gaziantep Turkish Super Lig form:.

Gaziantep form (all competitions):.

Amed SK Turkish Super Lig form:.

Amed SK form (all competitions):.

Gaziantep are expected to be without Fuat Bavuk, who is dealing with a hamstring injury, and Nazim Sangare, who has a back problem.

Serdar Dursun, Sontje Hansen, Arda Kizildag, Ulrich Meleke and Oguz Ozcecik are also listed as doubts, although their availability will need to be assessed closer to kickoff.

Amed will be without Samuel Ballet, who will serve the third of his three-game suspension, while Dilhan Demir and Lumbardh Dellova are dealing with injuries.

Gift Orban will be carrying much of the responsibility in attack as he looks to return to the scoresheet after failing to find the net last time out, while Dia Saba offers support behind him.

Gaziantep possible starting lineup:.

Tobiasz; Sorescu, Kizildag, Abena, Sarikaya; Meleke; Kozlowski, Gidado, Maxim, Camara; Dervisoglu.

Amed SK possible starting lineup:.

Lafont; Krasniqi, Yesil, Bates, Meras; Raveloson, Soyalp; Lutin, Saba, Sor; Orban.

Gaziantep's poor run of results and inability to win at home make it difficult to back them to turn things around against an Amed SK side that has shown considerably more attacking quality throughout the campaign.

The visitors look better equipped to secure all three points, and a narrow away victory appears the most likely outcome.

Liverpool have once again shown their flair for snapping up some of the most exciting teenagers in world football.

The Reds have made a happy habit of procuring some precocious up-and-coming talents in recent years, including the likes of Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni and Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

The Anfield hierarchy are at it again, with a deal in place to sign one of the stars of the ongoing Under-17 World Cup in Qatar.

As per James Pearce for The Athletic, Liverpool have secured an option to sign Senegalese winger Sidy Barhama Ndiaye when he turns 18, with the forward having been on trial with the Merseyside giants last year.

Currently playing for Diambars FC in his homeland, the 16-year-old’s performances have attracted interest from numerous European clubs, but it’s the Reds who’ve won the race for his services, having successfully negotiated an option to sign him in January 2028.

The teenager’s potential was spotted by LFC’s global talent team, who moved quickly to snap him up.

It has been revealed that want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Ndiaye was one of the standout performers for Senegal in their 9-0 trouncing of Cuba at the Under-17 World Cup earlier this week, scoring one goal and supplying two assists as his nation ran riot.

According to recent reports, given his nationality and the position that he plays, comparisons with Sadio Mane will be inevitable. If he can go on to have even half the impact that his compatriot enjoyed at Liverpool between 2016 and 2022 (120 goals in 269 appearances), he’ll be adored by the Kop.

Securing his signature will come as a huge fillip for the Reds’ recruitment staff, who’ve snapped up some outstanding young gems in recent years and hopefully have landed another one in Ndiaye.

It’ll obviously be a few years yet before the Senegalese prodigy makes his mark at Anfield, but the early signs are that this represents another terrific coup by LFC.
